belongs_to: Figure it Out Q1: "In the two rows below, colours repeat as shown. When will the blue stars meet next?"
description: Two horizontal rows of 12 five-pointed stars each, one above the other, stars of the two rows aligned in columns 1 to 12, each row followed on the right by a bold ellipsis (...) meaning the pattern continues. Row 1 (top) repeats a 6-colour block: yellow, green, orange, blue, pink, grey, then again yellow, green, orange, blue, pink, grey (stars 1-12); blue stars at positions 4 and 10. Row 2 (bottom) repeats a 4-colour block three times: green, orange, yellow, blue, | green, orange, yellow, blue, | green, orange, yellow, blue (stars 1-12); blue stars at positions 4, 8 and 12. Both rows have a blue star at position 4 (the first meeting); within the 12 printed stars the other blues (row 1: 10; row 2: 8, 12) do not line up. Colours used: yellow, green, orange, blue, pink (magenta), grey; stars are plain flat-coloured, no numbers or labels.

belongs_to: Puzzle Time 'Mystery Colours!': "The picture below shows all the designs for the numbers from 1 to 100. Try to decode the colour scheme for each number."
description: A 10 x 10 grid of 100 small round 'ring' badges on a pale yellow-green panel, numbers 1 to 100 in reading order (row 1 = 1-10, left to right, row 2 = 11-20, ... row 10 = 91-100). Each badge is a thick coloured ring with a white centre holding the number in dark bold sans-serif digits. The ring is cut by thin white gaps into n equal arcs, where n is the number of prime factors of the number counted with repeats (so a prime is one unbroken ring, 4 = 2 arcs, 8 = 3 arcs, 16 = 4 arcs, 32 = 5 arcs, 64 = 6 arcs). Each arc is coloured by the prime it stands for: 2 = green, 3 = pink/magenta, 5 = orange/amber, 7 = dark blue, every prime from 11 up = red; the number 1 is a single grey ring. The arcs run clockwise in increasing order of prime, the first arc centred at the top (12 o'clock); with 2 arcs the first is the top half and the second the bottom half (gaps at 9 and 3 o'clock), with 4 arcs the gaps sit on the diagonals. A red arc carries a very small white label with its prime (e.g. 22 shows 11, 26 shows 13, 94 shows 47); a red full ring (a prime itself, e.g. 11, 13, 17) has no label. Arc colours per badge, in clockwise order (red(p) = red arc labelled p): Row 1: 1 = grey full ring; 2 = green full ring; 3 = pink full ring; 4 = green/green; 5 = orange full ring; 6 = green/pink; 7 = blue full ring; Prime-labelled composites (33 numbers): 22:11, 26:13, 33:11, 34:17, 38:19, 39:13, 44:11, 46:23, 51:17, 52:13, 55:11, 57:19, 58:29, 62:31, 65:13, 66:11, 68:17, 69:23, 74:37, 76:19, 77:11, 78:13, 82:41, 85:17, 86:43, 87:29, 88:11, 91:13, 92:23, 93:31, 94:47, 95:19, 99:11. No title, key or legend is printed inside the grid (the heading 'Mystery Colours!' and the owl banner are page art). The same ring design surrounds the page numbers of every page of the chapter (p.63 shows blue/pink/pink, p.64 six green arcs, p.65 orange + red labelled 13), which is what the puzzle text refers to; the activity asks the student to extend the scheme and colour the page numbers 101-110 (no figure printed for that).
unclear: The tiny prime labels on red arcs are only a few pixels high; the 33 labels listed were read from the zoomed picture and agree with each number's prime factorisation.

The arc order/start angle was read from many badges (2, 4, 6, 12, 20, 24, 28, 48, 54, 56, 60, 84, 90) and fits 'first arc centred at the top, clockwise, smallest prime first'; exact gap angles are approximate.
